slides.say: A breakfast stand offers six hot drinks and five pastries. A customer chooses one of each. If the drink is espresso, the pastry must be a croissant. With any other drink, any pastry is allowed. How many choices are possible?
So a choice is one drink and one pastry. And there's a rule only for espresso.
We'll solve it in two different ways. Let's start with the math way, with two cases, like in the lesson. Case one, the drink is espresso.
at: Case one, the drink is espresso

slides.say: The drink has one option, espresso. And then the pastry must be a croissant, also one option.
One times one is one choice.
Case two, any other drink. Six drinks minus espresso leaves five options.
With these drinks, any pastry is allowed. The croissant too. So five options.
Five times five is twenty-five choices.
A drink is espresso or it isn't, so the cases don't overlap. We add them. One plus twenty-five is twenty-six.

Careful here. The rule works one way only. Espresso needs a croissant, but a croissant still goes with any other drink. If you take the croissant away from the other drinks, you get five times four plus one, twenty-one. That's choice number two, a trap.
[pause] Now let's count it the other way, all minus forbidden. With no rule at all, six drinks times five pastries is thirty.
Which choices does the rule forbid? Espresso with a pastry that isn't a croissant. There are four such pastries, so four forbidden choices.
Thirty minus four is twenty-six. The same answer.
Choice number three is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number three is our answer
